questions.solution:
**SOH-CAH-TOA:** $\sin = \dfrac{\text{O}}{\text{H}}$, $\cos = \dfrac{\text{A}}{\text{H}}$, $\tan = \dfrac{\text{O}}{\text{A}}$.

'Opposite' and 'adjacent' are always relative to the angle you are working with — they swap if you change angle.

In a right-angled isosceles triangle the two shorter sides are equal, so opposite $=$ adjacent and $\tan 45° = \mathbf{1}$.

Worth knowing exactly: $\sin 30° = \tfrac12$, $\cos 60° = \tfrac12$, $\tan 60° = \sqrt3$, $\sin 45° = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$.

The **sine rule** pairs each side with the angle opposite it.

Use it when you have a side and its opposite angle, plus one more piece of information. The second option is the **cosine rule**, used when you have two sides and the angle between them, or all three sides.

questions.q: The area of a triangle with sides $a$ and $b$ and included angle $C$ is:
questions.solution:
$\text{Area} = \mathbf{\dfrac12 ab\sin C}$.

The angle must be the one **between** the two sides. At $C = 90°$, $\sin C = 1$ and it reduces to the familiar $\tfrac12 \times$ base $\times$ height.

questions.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point on the ground is the angle between:
questions.solution:
It is measured **from the horizontal, upwards** to the line of sight.

The **angle of depression** is measured from the horizontal downwards, and the two are equal for the same pair of points — alternate angles between parallel horizontals.
options: the horizontal and the line of sight to the top
the vertical and the line of sight

questions.q: In a right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse is $10$ cm and one angle is $30°$. Find the side opposite that angle, in cm.
questions.solution:
$\sin 30° = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{10} \Rightarrow \text{opposite} = 10 \times 0.5 = \mathbf{5}$ cm.

In a $30$–$60$–$90$ triangle the shortest side is always exactly half the hypotenuse.

questions.q: In a right-angled triangle, the opposite side is $3$ cm and the adjacent $4$ cm. Find the angle, in degrees, correct to one decimal place.
questions.solution:
$\tan\theta = \dfrac34 = 0.75$

$\theta = \tan^{-1}(0.75) = \mathbf{36.9°}$.

The $3$–$4$–$5$ triangle has angles of about $36.9°$ and $53.1°$ — worth recognising on sight.

questions.q: Find the area (in cm$^{2}$) of a triangle with sides $6$ cm and $8$ cm and an included angle of $30°$.
In triangle $ABC$, $b = 5$, $c = 8$ and $A = 60°$. Find $a$, correct to two decimal places.
questions.solution:
$a^{2} = b^{2} + c^{2} - 2bc\cos A = 25 + 64 - 2(5)(8)(0.5) = 89 - 40 = 49$.

$a = \mathbf{7}$.

At $A = 60°$, $\cos A = \tfrac12$, so the correction term is exactly $bc$ — one of the reasons $60°$ appears so often in textbook questions.

questions.q: A tower is $30$ m tall. From a point $30$ m from its base, find the angle of elevation of its top, in degrees.
questions.solution:
$\tan\theta = \dfrac{30}{30} = 1 \Rightarrow \theta = \mathbf{45°}$.

Equal height and distance always gives $45°$ — worth using as a quick sanity check on any elevation answer.

questions.q: In triangle $ABC$, $A = 40°$, $B = 75°$ and $a = 12$ cm. Find $b$ and the third angle.
questions.solution:
**Third angle:**

$C = 180 - 40 - 75 = \mathbf{65°}$.

**Sine rule:**

$\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B}$

$b = \dfrac{a\sin B}{\sin A} = \dfrac{12 \times \sin 75°}{\sin 40°} = \dfrac{12 \times 0.9659}{0.6428}$

$b = \mathbf{18.03}$ cm.

**Sanity check:** $B$ is the largest angle, so $b$ should be the longest side — and $18.03 > 12$ ✓

The biggest side always faces the biggest angle, which catches most sine-rule slips before they cost a mark.

questions.q: In triangle $PQR$, $p = 7$ cm, $q = 9$ cm and $r = 12$ cm. Find the largest angle, correct to one decimal place.
questions.solution:
The **largest angle** is opposite the **longest side**, so it is $R$, opposite $r = 12$.

**Cosine rule rearranged:**

$\cos R = \dfrac{p^{2} + q^{2} - r^{2}}{2pq} = \dfrac{49 + 81 - 144}{2(7)(9)} = \dfrac{-14}{126} = -0.1111$

$R = \cos^{-1}(-0.1111) = \mathbf{96.4°}$.

**Reading the sign.** A **negative** cosine means an **obtuse** angle, so the triangle is obtuse-angled — which the numbers already hinted at, since $12^{2} = 144$ exceeds $7^{2} + 9^{2} = 130$.

That comparison is a quick test in itself: if the square of the longest side is greater than the sum of the other two squares, the triangle is obtuse; equal, and it is right-angled.

questions.q: From the top of a cliff $80$ m high, the angles of depression of two boats in line with the foot of the cliff are $30°$ and $45°$. Find the distance between the boats. Take $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$.
questions.solution:
Let the foot of the cliff be $F$, the top $T$, and the boats $A$ (further) and $B$ (nearer).

The angle of depression from $T$ equals the angle of elevation from the boat — alternate angles between two horizontals.

**Nearer boat ($45°$):**

$\tan 45° = \dfrac{80}{FB} \Rightarrow FB = \dfrac{80}{1} = 80$ m.

**Further boat ($30°$):**

$\tan 30° = \dfrac{80}{FA} \Rightarrow FA = \dfrac{80}{\tan 30°} = 80\sqrt3 = 80 \times 1.732 = 138.56$ m.

**Distance between the boats:**

$AB = FA - FB = 138.56 - 80 = \mathbf{58.56}$ m.

**Which angle goes with which boat?** The **smaller** angle of depression belongs to the **further** boat — a distant object is seen closer to the horizontal. Getting that the wrong way round gives a negative distance, which is at least an obvious warning.

**Check:** both boats are on the same side, so the distances subtract. Had they been on opposite sides of the cliff, they would have added.

questions.q: A vertical mast stands at a corner of a horizontal rectangular field $30$ m by $40$ m. The angle of elevation of the top of the mast from the opposite corner is $20°$. Find the height of the mast. Take $\tan 20° = 0.364$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — find the diagonal of the field**, which is the horizontal distance from the mast's base to the opposite corner:

$d = \sqrt{30^{2} + 40^{2}} = \sqrt{900 + 1600} = \sqrt{2500} = 50$ m.

**Step 2 — use the elevation** in the vertical triangle formed by the mast, the diagonal, and the line of sight:

$\tan 20° = \dfrac{h}{50}$

$h = 50 \times 0.364 = \mathbf{18.2}$ m.

**The method for every 3D question:** find the right-angled triangle that contains what you want, and get whatever horizontal distance it needs from a **separate** horizontal triangle first.

Two flat triangles, taken in the right order, solve a problem that looks three-dimensional. Sketching each one separately, out of the 3D picture, is what makes it manageable.

questions.q: Describe the graphs of $y = \sin x$ and $y = \cos x$ for $0° \le x \le 360°$, giving their maxima, minima and zeros.
questions.solution:
**$y = \sin x$**

• Starts at $(0, 0)$

• **Maximum** $1$ at $x = 90°$

• **Zero** again at $x = 180°$

• **Minimum** $-1$ at $x = 270°$

• Back to $0$ at $x = 360°$

**$y = \cos x$**

• Starts at $(0, 1)$

• **Zero** at $x = 90°$

• **Minimum** $-1$ at $x = 180°$

• **Zero** at $x = 270°$

• Back to $1$ at $x = 360°$

**Both** have amplitude $1$, period $360°$, and range $-1 \le y \le 1$. The cosine graph is the sine graph shifted **left by $90°$** — they are the same wave, started at different points.

**Why the graphs matter:** an equation such as $\sin x = 0.5$ has **two** solutions in $0°$ to $360°$ ($30°$ and $150°$), and a calculator gives only one. The graph shows you where the other is.
